search_result.content: How to Measure Couch Cushions for Replacement Fabrica Kraft。How to Measure Couch Cushions for Replacement A step-by-step guide to measuring sofa seat and back cushions, including T-cushions and odd shapes, so your replacements fit the frame the first time. Couch cushions take a lot of daily wear. Over time they flatten, lose their shape, or simply stop looking the way they did when the sofa was new. Replacing them is one of the easiest ways to bring a couch back to life, and the most important part of the job is getting the measurements right. This guide walks you through how to measure seat and back cushions so your new ones fit the frame snugly, look tailored, and feel comfortable from day one. What You Will Need Gather a few simple tools before you start: A rigid metal tape measure (a soft sewing tape helps on curves) A notepad or your phone to record numbers A large sheet of paper or cardboard if your cushions have an unusual shape Measure in inches and round to the nearest quarter inch. Write down every number as you go, and label each cushion so you don't mix them up later. Measure the Cushion or the Frame? If your existing cushions still hold their shape, measuring them is usually the fastest route. If they have shrunk, slumped, or gone missing, measure the space on the couch frame instead. Frame measurements tell you the true size of the opening the cushion needs to fill. When in doubt, measure both. If the cushion and the frame disagree by more than half an inch, trust the frame. How to Measure a Seat Cushion Width. Measure from the left side to the right side across the front edge of the cushion, seam to seam. Depth. Measure from the front edge to the back edge, through the middle of the cushion. Thickness. Measure the height of the side panel, not the puffy center. Rest a book lightly on top to get a true reading. Back width. Measure across the back edge too. Many sofa cushions are wider at the front than the back, especially on end seats. Shape notes. Note any T-shape, rounded corners, or angled sides. For a T-cushion, measure the full front width, the width at the back, and the depth of each "ear" that wraps in front of the arm. How to Measure a Back Cushion Width. Measure side to side across the widest point. Height. Measure from the bottom edge, where it sits on the seat cushion, up to the top edge. Thickness. Measure the side panel at the bottom and at the top. Back cushions are often thinner at the top, which helps them lean naturally against the frame. Tips for Measuring an Odd Shape Curved sofas, corner seats, and cushions that wrap around arms can be tricky. The easiest fix is a paper template. Lay a sheet of paper or flattened cardboard on the seat deck, press it into the corners, and trace the outline. Then measure the template and note where each curve starts and ends. A photo of the template next to a tape measure makes a handy reference. Common Mistakes to Avoid Measuring the crown. The center of an old cushion often bulges. Always measure thickness at the seam. Assuming every cushion is the same. End cushions often differ from middle ones. Measure each one separately. Including the piping. Measure seam to seam, not from the outer edge of any welt or piping, so you don't add extra width. Rushing. Measure twice. It takes a minute and saves a lot of hassle. Choosing Thickness and Fill Most sofa seat cushions fall somewhere between 4 and 6 inches thick. Our sofa and deep seat cushions can be made from 3 to 6 inches thick, so you can match your current cushions or go a little fuller. For indoor sofas, our High Density, Luxury, and Super Soft foam options let you choose anything from a firm, supportive seat to a softer, sink-in feel. If the couch lives on a porch or patio, Dry Fast foam drains water and is the better fit for outdoor use. You can compare every option in our custom foam collection. Picking a Fabric Indoors, you can choose from Warwick fabrics, velvet, and faux leather. For a busy family room or any outdoor seating, Sunbrella is a smart pick. It is a solution-dyed acrylic that holds its color in the sun and resists mildew. Every cover has a zipper, so it comes off when you need it to. Ready to Order? Once you have your numbers, head to our replacement couch cushions builder. Enter your measurements, pick your foam and fabric, and you'll see the price as you build. Every cushion is made to your exact size. In-stock fabrics ship in about 2 weeks, others in about 4 weeks, and shipping is free.

A step-by-step guide to measuring seat, back, tapered, chaise and bench cushions so your replacements fit first time. Step 1: Measure the foam, not the cover Step 2: Width, depth and thickness Step 3: Check the shape Step 4: Seat and back cushions Step 5: When the foam is flat or missing Step 6: Note the details How accurate will my cushion be? Ready to order? Frequently asked questions Should I measure the old cushion or the furniture? Do I measure seam to seam or edge to edge? Should I round up or down? Are seat and back cushions ordered together? What if my cushion is an unusual shape? Quick answer: Take the cover off and measure the foam edge to edge: width (side to side), depth (front to back) and thickness. Measure every cushion separately, give both widths for tapered seats, and measure seat and back cushions as separate items. If the foam is flat or missing, measure the furniture frame where the cushion sits instead. Round to the nearest ¼″. Most fit problems with replacement cushions come from measuring the wrong thing. Old covers stretch and old foam shrinks, so a quick measurement over the cover can be off by an inch or more. This guide shows exactly what to measure for each type of cushion. What you need A rigid tape measure (a soft sewing tape is easier on curves) Paper or cardboard for any curved or angled cushion A phone to photograph tricky shapes with the tape in the frame Step 1: Measure the foam, not the cover Unzip the cover and measure the foam itself, edge to edge. Covers are sewn seam to seam to fit the foam, so the foam is the true size. If your cushion has a Dacron (polyester fiber) wrap, measure the foam under it and do not reduce your measurements to allow for the wrap. Step 2: Width, depth and thickness Width: side to side, across the front edge. Depth: front edge to back edge, through the center. Thickness: top to bottom. Dining seats are usually 2–3″; deep-seat sofas 5–6″. Step 3: Check the shape Tapered (trapezoid) seats: measure the front width and the back width separately, then the depth. Use our trapezoid cushion builder. T-cushions: measure the full front width, the back width, the overall depth and the depth of the side “ears”. L-shaped and corner benches: measure the front, the overall depth, the back width and the depth of the short side. See the L-shaped builder. Round seats: measure across the widest point, then again at a right angle. If the two differ by more than ¼″, the seat is oval. Curves and cutouts: trace the cushion on paper and send a photo with a tape measure in the frame. Step 4: Seat and back cushions Measure seat and back cushions as separate items. For backs, measure width, height and thickness at both the top and bottom if they taper. For a hinged chaise cushion, measure the seat section and the back section separately and add them for the total length. Step 5: When the foam is flat or missing Measure the frame where the cushion sits: inside the arms for width, and from the front rail to the back for depth. A snug fit looks best, so do not add extra. For benches with arms, measure between the arms. Step 6: Note the details Where ties go (usually the back corners) and how many Zipper position (usually the back or hinged side) Piping (also called welting), if you want it Notches for posts, chains or rope on swings How accurate will my cushion be? We cut every Fabrica Kraft cushion to within ±0.5″ of your measurements, and most orders ship in 2–3 weeks. Custom cushions are made to your size and cannot be returned, so it is worth measuring twice. If a cushion arrives outside that tolerance, we remake it. Ready to order? Start with replacement cushions for outdoor furniture, or order covers only if your foam is still in good shape. Frequently asked questions Should I measure the old cushion or the furniture? Measure the old foam if it still holds its shape. If it is flat, crumbly or missing, measure the furniture frame where the cushion sits. Do I measure seam to seam or edge to edge? Measure the foam edge to edge. Covers are sewn seam to seam to fit that foam. Should I round up or down? Round to the nearest ¼″. If you are measuring a frame with sides on all four edges, rounding down by about ¼″ helps the cushion drop in without bowing. Are seat and back cushions ordered together?

search_result.content: How to Measure Replacement Garden Cushions Correctly (Step-by-Step Guide) PatioCushions。How to Measure Replacement Garden Cushions Correctly (Step-by-Step Guide) If you’re looking for replacement garden cushions, getting the measurements right is the most important step. Even a few centimetres can make the difference between a perfect fit and cushions that look untidy or slide around every time you sit down. In this guide, we’ll show you exactly how to measure your existing cushions or outdoor furniture to ensure your new cushions fit perfectly. Why Accurate Measurements Matter Garden furniture comes in hundreds of different shapes and sizes. Even furniture that looks identical can often have slightly different dimensions. Correct measurements help you: Achieve a neat, professional look Improve comfort and support Prevent cushions from moving around Avoid costly mistakes and returns Get the most from custom-made cushions What You’ll Need Before you start measuring, grab: A tape measure A notebook or phone for notes A camera (optional but helpful) For best results, use a flexible tape measure rather than a rigid ruler. Measuring Seat Cushions For seat cushions, you need three measurements: Width Measure from one side of the seat to the other. 📏 Example: 120 cm Depth Measure from the front edge of the seat to the back. 📏 Example: 60 cm Thickness Measure the height of the cushion from top to bottom. 📏 Example: 10 cm or 15 cm Example size: 120 × 60 × 10 cm Measuring Back Cushions Back cushions are measured slightly differently. Width Measure across the cushion from side to side. Height Measure from the bottom to the top. Thickness Measure the depth of the cushion. Example size: 60 × 40 × 10 cm Measuring Rattan Furniture Cushions If your old cushions are missing or worn out, measure the furniture itself. For rattan furniture: Measure the internal seating area Measure between the arms Measure the usable depth Check if corners are rounded Many rattan furniture sets have slight variations, even within the same collection. Measuring Pallet Sofa Cushions Pallet furniture is usually made from standard Euro pallets. Common sizes include: Cushion Type Typical Size Seat Cushion 120 × 80 cm Seat Cushion 120 × 60 cm Back Cushion 120 × 40 cm Back Cushion 60 × 40 cm Always measure your pallet seating before ordering, as DIY pallet furniture often varies. Measuring Corner Sofa Cushions For corner units, measure each section separately. Record: Left section Corner section Right section Do not assume both sides are identical. A simple sketch with dimensions can help avoid confusion when ordering custom cushions. Measuring Bench Cushions For bench cushions, measure: Length Depth Desired thickness Popular bench cushion depths are: 30 cm 35 cm 40 cm 45 cm For window seats, measure the recess carefully and check whether the corners are square or rounded. Should You Measure Existing Cushions or Furniture? If your current cushions fit perfectly, measure the cushions. If your cushions are old, sagging, misshapen or missing, measure the furniture instead. Furniture measurements are usually the more reliable option for replacement cushions. Common Measuring Mistakes Measuring Curved Cushions Incorrectly Always measure the widest points. Forgetting the Thickness Many customers remember length and width but forget thickness. A 10 cm cushion feels very different from a 15 cm cushion. Measuring from the Wrong Position Measure the actual seating area, not the overall furniture frame. Guessing Never estimate measurements. Even small errors can affect the final fit. Need Custom-Made Garden Cushions? At Patio Cushions, we manufacture custom replacement cushions for: Rattan furniture Garden sofas Pallet furniture Benches Conservatories Caravan seating If you’re unsure about your measurements, simply send us a few photos and the dimensions you have, and we’ll be happy to help. Final Thoughts Taking accurate measurements only takes a few minutes, but it ensures your replacement cushions fit beautifully and provide the comfort you’re looking for. When in doubt, measure twice, write everything down, and take a few photos before ordering. A little extra care at this stage can save a lot of time and frustration later.

search_result.content: How to Take Precise Measurements for Custom Replacement Cushions Kraft Cushions。How to Take Precise Measurements for Custom Replacement Cushions Measuring for custom replacement cushions is the single most important step in giving your outdoor or indoor furniture a fresh, tailored update. Whether your old cushions are sagging, faded, or completely worn out, getting precise dimensions ensures your new set fits snugly without bunching, overhanging, or shifting. Follow this step-by-step guide to take exact measurements for your furniture before ordering. Phase 1: Preparation & Essential Tools Before taking a single measurement, gather the right tools and prepare your furniture: Use a Rigid Metal Measuring Tape: Flexible cloth tailor's tapes stretch over time and lead to inaccurate readings. Stick to a standard steel tape measure. Remove Old Cushions: Never measure existing cushions. Over time, foam degrades, flattens, and shifts, while fabric covers stretch out. Always measure the furniture frame itself. Grab Paper and a Pen: Sketch a top-down diagram of each seating surface to write measurements directly alongside the corresponding edges. Phase 2: Measuring Standard Seat Cushions For standard square or rectangular deep-seating chairs, loveseats, and sofas, you need three key dimensions: Width, Depth, and Thickness. +-----------------------+ | WIDTH | | (Side-to-Side Space) | +-----------------------+ | | D | | E | | P | | T | | H | | +-----------------------+ Width (Side-to-Side): Measure the inside distance of the seating area from the left inner wall/arm to the right inner wall/arm. Fit Adjustment: If your furniture has solid side walls, subtract $1/2$ inch from the total width to allow the cushion to slide in easily without bulging. Depth (Front-to-Back): Measure from the inside back frame to the front edge of the seat rail. Thickness (Height): Determine how tall you want your cushion to be (typically 3 to 6 inches). Ensure the thickness allows your legs to rest comfortably on the ground when seated. Phase 3: Measuring Back Cushions Measuring back cushions requires special attention to how they interact with the seat cushions. +-----------------------+ | BACK FRAME HEIGHT | +-----------------------+ | | | | BACK CUSHION HEIGHT | | Total Frame | | | Height +-----------------------+ | | SEAT CUSHION HEIGHT | | ======================================= (Base Frame) Back Cushion Width: Measure the inside width of the back frame. This is usually identical to the seat cushion width. Back Cushion Height: Measure from the top of the seat frame to the top of the back frame. Crucial Step: Subtract the thickness of your new seat cushion. For example, if your back frame is 22 inches tall and your new seat cushion is 4 inches thick, your back cushion height should be 18 inches. Phase 4: Measuring Complex & Custom Shapes If your furniture features trapezoids, L-shapes, or curved corners, follow these steps to ensure accuracy: Shape Type Key Measurements Required Pro Tip Trapezoid / Tapered • Front Width • Back Width • Center Depth Measure both front and back widths separately, as inner back frames are often narrower than the front opening. L-Shaped Sectionals • Full Outer Lengths • Inner Corner Lengths • Individual Cushion Depths Break the sectional into separate rectangular blocks on a diagram before recording edges. Curved / Round Backs • Maximum Front Width • Depth at Center Point • Radius of Corner Curves Make a butcher paper template of the seat bottom and mail or upload it to your cushion fabricator. Common Pitfalls to Avoid Measuring Edge-to-Edge on Old Covers: Seams pull inward over time; measuring an old cover yields dimensions that are too small. Forgetting Tie Locations: If you need ties to keep outdoor cushions attached during windy weather, measure and mark the exact points on the frame where ties should attach (e.g., "3 inches from back left corner"). Ignoring Cushion Piping (Welting): If adding thick decorative piping around the edges, ensure your frame clearance accounts for an extra $1/8$ to $1/4$ inch along the perimeter. Summary Checklist Before Ordering [ ] Did you measure the furniture frame, not the old cushion? [ ] Did you use a rigid metal tape measure? [ ] Did you subtract the seat cushion thickness from the back cushion height? [ ] Did you deduct $1/2$ inch on width for tight, enclosed frames? [ ] Have you double-checked all numbers against your sketch?

search_result.content: How to Measure for Replacement Outdoor Cushions。Introduction As the seasons change, so does the wear and tear on your outdoor furniture. Replacing worn-out cushions can breathe new life into your patio set, making it both comfortable and visually appealing. However, measuring for replacement cushions can be a bit tricky. Here’s a comprehensive guide to help you get the perfect fit for your outdoor furniture. Gather Your Tools Before you start measuring, make sure you have the following tools on hand: Measuring tape (preferably one that’s flexible and not too rigid) Pen and paper (or a digital device to record measurements) The old cushion (if it’s still in reasonable shape) Understand Cushion Types There are generally three types of cushions you’ll be dealing with: seat cushions, back cushions, and chaise lounge cushions. Each requires specific measurements. Measuring Seat Cushions Measure the Width Place the measuring tape at the left edge of the seating area and extend it to the right edge. Write down the width measurement. Measure the Depth Measure from the front edge of the seat to the back where it meets the backrest. Record this measurement as well. Measure the Thickness If you have the old cushion, measure its thickness from the top to the bottom. If the old cushion is unavailable, an average thickness of 2 to 4 inches is typical for outdoor cushions. Measuring Back Cushions Measure the Width Measure the width of the backrest from one side to the other, following the same process as for the seat cushions. Measure the Height Measure from the top of the backrest to the point where it meets the seat. Measure the Thickness Again, if the old cushion is available, use it as a reference. If not, a typical back cushion thickness is around 3 to 5 inches. Measuring Chaise Lounge Cushions Chaise lounge cushions are a bit more complex due to their elongated shape and multiple segments. Measure the Length Measure the entire length of the chaise lounge from the top of the backrest to the bottom of the seat. Measure Each Segment If the cushion has distinct segments (backrest, seat, leg rest), measure each one separately. Record the width, length, and thickness for each segment. Additional Tips for Accurate Measurement Double-Check Your Measurements: Accuracy is key. Double-check each measurement to avoid mistakes. Consider Cushion Shape: Some cushions have rounded or angled edges. Note any irregular shapes and measure the widest points. Account for Fabric Stretch: Outdoor cushions may stretch over time, so consider this when measuring. Replacement Covers: If you’re only replacing the cushion covers, use the same measurements but allow for a snug fit. Custom vs. Standard Sizes While many outdoor furniture sets use standard cushion sizes, some might require custom-made cushions. If your measurements don’t match any standard sizes, consider ordering custom cushions. Many retailers offer custom options where you can input your exact measurements. Choosing the Right Material When replacing outdoor cushions, material choice is crucial. Look for weather-resistant fabrics like Sunbrella, which can withstand UV rays, moisture, and mildew. Ensure the filling is also designed for outdoor use, typically quick-drying foam or polyester fiberfill. Conclusion Measuring for replacement outdoor cushions doesn’t have to be daunting. With the right tools and careful measurement, you can find cushions that fit perfectly, enhancing the comfort and aesthetics of your outdoor space. Remember to take your time, double-check your measurements, and consider the material that best suits your climate and usage. Enjoy your revitalized outdoor living area!

search_result.content: How to Measure for Replacement Wicker Loveseat Cushions。If your current wicker loveseat cushions are faded, worn out, or no longer comfortable, replacing them is one of the fastest ways to refresh your furniture and improve your seating experience. But before you buy, accurate measurements are essential. The wrong size cushion can look awkward, shift around, or even cause premature wear on your wicker frame. Here’s a simple step-by-step guide to measuring your wicker loveseat so your new cushions fit perfectly. Table of Contents 1. Gather Your Tools All you need is: A flexible measuring tape A notepad and pen (or your phone) to record numbers Your current cushions (if you have them) for comparison 2. Measure the Seat Width Measure across the widest point of your loveseat’s seating area from left to right. For straight-edged loveseats, measure from arm to arm. For curved or rounded designs, measure at both the front and back, then note the smaller number to ensure a snug fit. Write this down as your seat width. 3. Measure the Seat Depth Measure from the front edge of the seat to where it meets the backrest. If your wicker loveseat has a curved back, measure the center depth and side depths to get an accurate range. For a plush, comfortable look, you can subtract ½ inch to avoid cushions that overhang the edge. 4. Measure the Back Height (if applicable) If your wicker loveseat cushions include back cushions, measure from the seat base to the top of the backrest. This ensures you don’t end up with cushions that look too short or overwhelm the frame. 5. Trace the seat shape on paper or cardboard for reference if ordering custom cushions. When in doubt, send these measurements and a photo to the manufacturer. 6. Don’t Forget Cushion Thickness Cushion thickness affects comfort and aesthetics. Most wicker loveseat cushions range from 3″ to 6″ thick. Thicker cushions give a plush look but can raise the seating height. Thinner cushions maintain the original profile but may offer less support. Final Tip Always double-check your measurements before ordering. If you’re replacing old cushions, compare your measurements with the originals—especially if the old ones have flattened over time. With precise measurements, you’ll get wicker loveseat cushions that not only fit like a glove but also breathe new life into your furniture, making your loveseat as inviting as the day you bought it.

One side might sag more than the other, creating that uncomfortable “hammock” effect. Sometimes, the foam itself is fine, but the inner wrapping-often made of polyester fiberfill or Dacron batting-has flattened. This outer layer provides the plush feel on top of the firm foam core. If only the batting is worn, you might save money by having an upholsterer re-wrap the existing foam rather than replacing the entire block. Measuring for Replacement Cushions: The Critical Step The biggest mistake people make is assuming all sofa cushions are standard sizes. They aren’t. To replace them successfully, you need precise measurements. Grab a tape measure and follow these steps: Measure the length: Place the tape along the longest edge of the cushion, from corner to corner. Do this while the cushion is uncompressed if possible, but note that some compression is inevitable during measurement. Measure the width: Measure the shortest edge, again from corner to corner. Measure the height: This is tricky. Sit on the sofa normally, then measure from the base of the seat (where the cushion sits) to the top of the cushion at its highest point. Remember to account for any skirt or piping that might add extra height. Check the corners: Are they square, rounded, or tapered? Tapered corners require custom fabrication because they won’t fit into a box-style frame. Write these numbers down clearly. Even a half-inch discrepancy can result in cushions that look sloppy or don’t fit properly in the sofa’s track system. Foam Density Matters More Than Thickness Not all foam is created equal. When ordering replacements, you’ll encounter terms like “density” and “ILD” (Indentation Load Deflection). These numbers determine how long your new cushions will last and how they feel under pressure. Property Low End (Budget) Middle Ground (Standard) High End (Premium) Density (kg/m³) 18-25 kg/m³ 30-40 kg/m³ 45+ kg/m³ ILD Rating 1.5-2.0 lbs 2.5-3.5 lbs 4.0+ lbs Lifespan Estimate 1-2 years 3-5 years 7+ years Feel Soft, quick rebound Balanced support Firm, supportive Foam Density and ILD Comparison for Sofa Cushions If you’re replacing cushions for a family room where kids jump on the sofa, aim for at least 30 kg/m³ density. For a formal living room used occasionally, lower density might suffice. Higher ILD means firmer support, which is better for older adults who need help standing up from a seated position. Options for Replacement: DIY vs. Professional Upholstery You have three main paths forward, each with different costs and effort levels. Option 1: Buy Pre-Made Cushions Online This works only if your sofa has very standard dimensions. Many online retailers sell generic sofa cushions in common sizes like 20x20 inches or 24x24 inches. Check if your cushions match these exactly. If they do, you can order them directly. However, most sofas have unique shapes or non-standard depths, making this option unlikely to yield a perfect fit. Option 2: Hire a Local Upholsterer This is often the best route for quality and longevity. An experienced upholsterer can assess whether your existing foam is salvageable. If so, they can add fresh Dacron batting to restore the plush surface. If the foam is dead, they’ll cut new blocks to your exact specifications and wrap them professionally. In New Zealand, labor costs vary, but expect to pay between $80 and $150 per cushion depending on complexity. While pricier upfront, this solution typically lasts longer than DIY attempts. Option 3: DIY Foam Cutting and Wrapping If you’re handy, you can buy raw foam sheets and Dacron batting yourself. Cut the foam using a serrated knife or electric cutter, ensuring clean edges. Then, wrap the foam tightly with batting, securing it with spray adhesive or staples. Finally, sew a new cover or reuse the old one if it’s still in good condition. This approach saves money but requires patience and precision. Mistakes in cutting lead to lopsided cushions that look amateurish. What About the Covers? Replacing the foam doesn’t mean you must replace the fabric covers. If your current covers are stained, torn, or outdated, consider reupholstering them simultaneously. Fabric choice impacts durability and comfort. Microfiber resists stains well, while linen offers breathability but wrinkles easily. Velvet adds luxury but shows wear patterns quickly. Consult with your upholsterer about fabric weight and stretch properties to ensure the new cover fits snugly over the refreshed cushion. If you keep the original covers, check the zippers and seams. Worn zippers can tear delicate fabrics during removal and reinstallation. Reinforce weak spots before proceeding. Cost Breakdown: Is It Worth It?

Step 1: Measure The Width Width is measured from left to right across the furniture frame. How To Measure Width: Use a rigid tape measure. Measure the width across the front of the seat frame. search_result.content: How to Measure Foam for Replacement Cushions: A Step-by-Step Guide Royal Shade USA。 Imagine your original sofa cushion contained a 4-inch-thick foam insert. After years of daily use, that foam may have permanently compressed. If you measure only the worn foam, you could unintentionally order a thinner replacement. Instead: Remove the old foam. Lay the cushion cover flat. Measure seam to seam. Compare those measurements with the old foam. Look for signs of compression or deformation. This gives you a much better picture of the dimensions the replacement foam needs to fill. What About Dacron or Polyester Batting? When removing your old cushion insert, you may discover that the foam is surrounded by a soft layer of polyester batting, often referred to as Dacron wrap. This layer can help: Soften the edges of the foam Create a fuller cushion appearance Reduce visible sharp corners Help fill out the cushion cover Produce a more rounded or "crowned" appearance However, don't automatically include the thickness of the batting when determining the dimensions of the foam core. The foam and batting perform different functions. For example, a cushion may have a 4-inch foam core with batting wrapped around it. Measuring the finished cushion at its thickest point could therefore make the insert appear significantly thicker than the actual foam. Measuring Different Cushion Shapes Not every cushion is a simple rectangle. Custom furniture often requires more detailed measurements. Square and Rectangular Cushions These are the easiest. Record: Width × Depth × Thickness For example: 26" × 24" × 4" This format works well for: Couch cushions Bench cushions Window seats Dining chairs Patio furniture RV seating Royal Shade's Custom Cut High Density Foam can be ordered for standard rectangular applications as well as various custom shapes. T-Shaped Cushions T-cushions are commonly found on sofas and armchairs where part of the cushion extends around the furniture's arm. For these cushions, measure: Overall width Overall depth Thickness Width of the rear section Depth of each extension Position of the cut-ins A simple sketch with every dimension labeled can help prevent mistakes. L-Shaped Cushions L-shaped cushions are frequently used for: Sectional sofas Corner benches Breakfast nooks Built-in seating Measure the overall dimensions first, then measure each section of the "L" independently. Create a top-view drawing and label every straight edge. This is much safer than submitting only the maximum width and depth. Round Cushions For a circular cushion, measure: Diameter × Thickness Measure the diameter across the widest point of the circle. For example: 20" Diameter × 3" Thick Curved or Irregular Cushions For curved, trapezoid, oval, or unusually shaped cushions, measurements alone may not always communicate the shape accurately. In these situations, consider creating a full-size paper template. Place the original cushion or furniture seating area on kraft paper or another large sheet and carefully trace the outline. Clearly mark: Front Back Left Right Thickness Important corners or curves Royal Shade offers custom foam cutting beyond simple rectangles, including round, oval, L-shaped, triangle, and other custom configurations. See the Royal Shade Custom Foam product page for available customization options. How Much Bigger Should Replacement Foam Be Than the Cover? This is where measurement becomes slightly more complicated. In some upholstery applications, the foam may be cut slightly larger than the measured cushion cover so that the finished cushion looks full rather than loose. However, there is no single oversizing rule that should be applied to every cushion. The correct allowance can depend on: Foam thickness Cover construction Fabric stretch Existing batting Desired firmness Cushion shape Whether Dacron or another wrap will be added For example, FoamOrder's measuring guidance recommends different allowances depending on cushion thickness and whether batting will be used. Therefore, when ordering custom replacement foam, check the foam supplier's sizing recommendations rather than automatically adding an arbitrary amount to every dimension. Common Mistakes When Measuring Replacement Cushion Foam 1. Measuring Only the Old Foam Old foam may have compressed significantly. Better approach: Compare the existing insert with seam-to-seam measurements of the cushion cover. 2. Measuring Across the Rounded Center The center of a cushion may be higher because of batting and the cushion's crown. Better approach: Measure thickness at the side seams or boxing. 3. Stretching the Fabric Stretching an empty cushion cover while measuring can create oversized dimensions. Better approach: Lay it flat and smooth it naturally. 4. Forgetting About Batting A finished cushion may be thicker than its foam core because of Dacron or polyester wrap. Better approach: Identify the foam core and batting as separate components. 5. Assuming Every Cushion Is Rectangular T-cushions, curved cushions, sectional cushions, and custom furniture often require additional dimensions. Better approach: Draw and label the cushion before ordering. 6. Measuring Only Once A ½-inch mistake can matter when you're ordering custom-cut foam. Better approach: Measure every dimension at least twice before submitting your order. Choosing the Right Foam for Replacement Cushions Measurements determine whether your replacement foam fits.

search_result.content: How to Measure RV Cushions for Replacement (Step-by-Step)。How to Measure RV Cushions for Replacement (Step-by-Step) TL;DR: To measure RV cushions for replacement, always measure the existing cushion (not the bench frame) in three dimensions: length, width, and thickness. Measure seam to seam, then add 0.5" to length and width so the foam fills the cover fully. For odd shapes like L-shapes, rounded corners, or U-shaped dinettes, trace a cardboard template or send a photo and we'll sketch it out before cutting anything. You finally decided to replace those flat, worn-out RV cushions. You grabbed a tape measure, you measured... something. Then your new cushions arrived and they didn't fit right. It happens more than you'd think. And almost every time, it comes down to one mistake: measuring the wrong thing. This guide will walk you through exactly how to measure custom RV cushions so your replacement arrives and fits perfectly the first time. No guesswork, no remakes. Do You Measure the RV Cushion or the Bench Frame? Measure your existing cushion, not the bench frame. The cushion and the frame are almost never the same size. A cushion is cut slightly larger than the frame so it fills the space with a snug, full look. If you measure the frame and order to that size, your new cushion will come in too small and look sunken. The only time you should measure the frame is when your old cushion is so badly deformed that it no longer holds its original shape. If it's collapsed, lumpy, or has been sitting wet, it may have shrunk or warped. In that case, measure the open bench space instead and let us know when you order. If your cushion is just flat or faded but still holds its general shape, measure the cushion. That's the right size. One customer from Florida asked us this exact question twice before ordering. "Do I measure the cushion or the frame inside for a camper couch?" Both times, the answer was the same: the cushion. When she ordered that way, everything fit perfectly. The 3 Numbers You Need To order a replacement RV cushion, you need exactly three measurements: length, width, and thickness. That's it. Here's how to get each one right. Length and width: measure seam to seam Place your cushion flat on the floor. Using a soft tape measure, measure from the stitched seam on one end to the stitched seam on the other end. Do this for both dimensions. Don't measure from the outer edge of any piping or trim. Measure to the seam itself. Once you have both numbers, add 0.5 inches to each dimension. So if your cushion measures 35.5" long, you order 36". This extra allowance means the foam will press firmly against the inside of the cover and give you that full, well-stuffed look instead of a saggy one. Thickness: use a ruler and the floor Don't try to measure thickness with a tape measure. It's too flexible and you'll get an inaccurate reading. Instead, lay the cushion flat on a hard surface like a wood floor or kitchen counter. Hold a rigid ruler or straightedge on top of the cushion so it extends past the edge. Then measure straight down from the underside of the ruler to the floor. That's your foam thickness. Write down all three numbers before you move to the next cushion. It sounds obvious, but it's easy to mix them up if you're measuring a whole dinette set. How to Measure Odd-Shaped RV Cushions RV cushions are rarely simple rectangles. If yours has rounded corners, an L-shape, a U-shape, or a trapezoid angle, measuring gets a little more involved. But it's still totally manageable. Rounded corners Measure the length and width as normal (seam to seam). Then measure the radius of the corner curve. A corner radius of 4–6 inches is common on RV dinettes. Write that down separately and note it when you order. L-shaped or U-shaped dinettes Break the shape into individual rectangular sections. Measure each section separately: its own length, width, and thickness. Also note where the sections meet and whether there's a seam or a hinge between them. One customer in Colorado needed 7 custom cushions for a U-shaped dinette. She sketched her layout by hand, labeled every measurement, and sent us the sketch. We turned it into a production diagram, confirmed every dimension with her, and shipped the full set in about three weeks. She told us: "They look great!

Adding a Dacron wrap? Order the foam at the exact seam-to-seam cover size. The wrap plumps up the rest and builds the crown. Not sure which applies? Contact us. search_result.content: How to Replace Outdoor Furniture Cushions: Complete Guide 2025 Cushion Atlas。How to Replace Outdoor Furniture Cushions: Complete Guide 2025 Replacing outdoor furniture cushions breathes new life into your patio or deck furniture while maintaining comfort and style. This comprehensive guide walks you through the entire process, from measuring and selecting materials to installation and maintenance, ensuring your outdoor space looks fresh and inviting for years to come. Table of Contents When to Replace Your Outdoor Furniture Cushions Knowing when to replace outdoor cushions saves money and prevents frustration. Signs of replacement include faded colors that won’t restore with cleaning, tears or holes larger than two inches, compressed foam that won’t bounce back, persistent odors despite thorough cleaning, and mold or mildew stains that resist treatment. Most high-quality outdoor cushions last 3-5 years with proper care. Weather damage accelerates deterioration, especially in regions with extreme temperatures or high humidity. UV exposure breaks down fabric fibers and foam materials, while moisture creates breeding grounds for mold and bacteria. Regular inspection during spring cleaning helps identify problems before they become irreparable. Measuring Your Outdoor Furniture for New Cushions Accurate measurements ensure perfect-fitting replacement cushions that provide optimal comfort and appearance. Start by measuring the length, width, and desired thickness of each cushion separately, as dimensions often vary slightly between pieces. Use a metal tape measure for precision, and record measurements to the nearest quarter-inch. For seat cushions, measure from the back of the frame to the front edge, then side to side at the widest point. Back cushions require height measurements from the seat to the top of the frame, plus width measurements. Consider the cushion thickness you prefer – typically 2-4 inches for seats and 3-6 inches for backs, depending on frame depth and personal comfort preferences. Tools Needed for Accurate Measuring Essential measuring tools include a metal tape measure (at least 25 feet long), notepad and pen for recording dimensions, and a digital camera to photograph furniture angles and attachment points. A flexible measuring tape helps with curved or angled surfaces, while a level ensures accurate measurements on uneven surfaces. Having a measuring assistant makes the process faster and more accurate, especially for large furniture pieces. Common Measuring Mistakes to Avoid Avoid measuring over existing cushions, which adds unwanted bulk to your calculations. Don’t assume all cushions on a set are identical – measure each piece individually. Failing to account for frame curvature or arm rests leads to poor-fitting replacements. Always double-check measurements and add notes about special features like ties, buttons, or welting that affect the final dimensions. Choosing the Right Materials for Outdoor Cushions Selecting appropriate outdoor cushion materials determines durability, comfort, and maintenance requirements. Fabric choices include solution-dyed acrylics like Sunbrella, which resist fading and moisture, polyester blends that offer affordability with decent weather resistance, and marine-grade vinyl for maximum waterproofing. Avoid indoor fabrics that deteriorate rapidly in outdoor conditions. Foam selection significantly impacts comfort and longevity. Quick-dry foam prevents mold growth by allowing moisture to drain through, while standard polyurethane foam requires waterproof covers to prevent deterioration. When to Replace Your Cushions Cushions don't need to be replaced at the first sign of wear. Before buying replacements, assess what's actually wrong: Faded colour: UV fading is normal over time. If the cushion is structurally sound and the cover is removable, try washing the cover first — fading often looks worse when the fabric is dirty. If the colour is genuinely gone, a new cover is the most cost-effective fix. Flattened filling: cushion foam compresses over time with use. If the cover is in good condition but the cushion feels flat, the foam insert can be replaced independently — standard foam sheets are available from fabric shops and online. Cut to size and insert into the existing cover. Mildew: before replacing, try treating with a diluted white vinegar solution (1 part vinegar to 2 parts water), leave for 30 minutes, scrub gently and rinse. Dry fully in the sun. Mild mildew often comes out completely. Severe mildew that has penetrated the foam warrants replacement. Torn or damaged covers: if the cover is torn but the foam is fine, replace the cover only. If both are damaged, replace the full cushion. Standard Outsunny Cushion Sizes Outsunny doesn't publish a universal cushion size guide, and sizes vary across the range. However, most Outsunny sofa and lounge cushions fall within a set of standard dimensions that are widely available as universal replacements: Seat cushions (sofa sets and lounge chairs): 48cm x 48cm x 8cm — most common for mid-range corner sofa sets 50cm x 50cm x 8cm — common on larger sofa sets 55cm x 55cm x 8cm — found on some premium sets 60cm x 60cm x 8cm — larger lounge chairs and some corner sets Back cushions (sofa sets): 48cm x 48cm x 8cm — most common 50cm x 50cm x 8cm — common on larger sets Dining chair cushions: 40cm x 40cm x 5cm — most common for dining chairs 45cm x 45cm x 5cm — found on some larger dining chairs Sun lounger cushions: these vary more significantly by model. Most Outsunny lounger cushions are 170–190cm long and 55–65cm wide. Measure your existing cushion or the lounger frame before ordering. Swing seat cushions: highly model-specific. For lounger cushions: measure the full length of the lounger frame from headrest to foot, and the width of the seat platform. The cushion should match the frame length and be 2–5cm narrower than the frame width to sit neatly within the sides. For swing seat cushions: measure the seat width and depth, and the backrest height. Swing seat cushions are often sold as a set (seat + back) — check whether you need both or just one. Depth matters: a replacement cushion that's thinner than the original will look and feel wrong. Aim to match the original depth as closely as possible — 8cm is the standard for mid-range Outsunny sofa sets. Compatibility: Exact Replacements vs Universal Fit Exact Outsunny replacement cushions are available directly from Outsunny and through some retailers. To find the right ones, you'll need your model number — usually found on a label on the frame or in the original assembly instructions. Exact replacements guarantee the right fit and matching fabric, but availability varies and older models may no longer have replacements in stock. Universal outdoor cushions in standard sizes (48x48cm, 50x50cm etc.) are widely available and often fit Outsunny frames well.

If the covers are in good shape, move on. Vacuum the inside of the covers. Use an upholstery attachment to remove foam crumbs, dust, and debris that have accumulated inside. This prevents the new insert from sitting on a lumpy bed of old particles. Position the insert. If your new cushion has a Dacron wrap, make sure the seam of the wrap faces the back of the cushion (not the seating surface). search_result.content: Expert Tips For Accurately Measuring Your Sofa Cushions For Perfect Covers。Replacing or refreshing your sofa cushion covers can dramatically transform the look of your living space. Ill-fitting covers bunch up, slip off, or stretch awkwardly—ruining both comfort and aesthetics. The key to success lies in precise measurement. Done right, accurate measurements ensure a tailored, snug fit that looks professionally installed. This guide delivers expert-backed techniques to help you measure every type of sofa cushion with confidence. Why Accurate Measurements Matter A common misconception is that standard sizes are sufficient when ordering replacement covers. In reality, sofa cushions—even from the same manufacturer—can vary by as much as half an inch due to wear, foam compression, or production inconsistencies. A cover that’s just slightly too small will strain at the seams; one that’s too large will sag and wrinkle. Custom-fit covers not only enhance visual appeal but also prolong the life of your cushions by reducing friction and movement. Additionally, accurate dimensions are essential when working with tailored fabrics like linen, velvet, or outdoor synthetics, which have limited stretch and require exact cuts. “Precision in measurement is non-negotiable. A 0.5-inch error can turn a sleek cover into a sloppy mess.” — Lena Torres, Upholstery Designer & Textile Consultant Essential Tools for Measuring Sofa Cushions Before taking any measurements, gather the right tools. Using improper instruments leads to inaccuracies that compound during fabrication. Tape measure: A flexible, metal tape measure (at least 60 inches) is ideal. Avoid cloth tapes, which stretch and give false readings. Notebook and pen: Record each dimension immediately to avoid confusion. Felt-tip marker: Use it to label cushions (e.g., “Left Back,” “Center Seat”) if they aren’t identical. Flat surface: Remove cushions and lay them on a level floor or table to prevent distortion during measurement. Tip: Measure each cushion individually—even those that appear identical. Wear and use cause subtle dimensional changes over time. Step-by-Step Guide to Measuring Different Cushion Types Sofa cushions come in various shapes and configurations. Follow these steps based on your cushion type for foolproof results. 1. Rectangular Seat Cushions Lay the cushion flat on a hard surface. Measure the length from left to right across the front edge. Measure the depth from front to back at the center. Measure the thickness (height) from top to bottom at the thickest point. Note seam allowances if the original cover had piping or welting (typically add ½ inch per side). 2. Back Cushions Back cushions often lean against the frame and may be tapered or contoured. Place the cushion upright or flat, depending on shape. Measure height from top to bottom at the center. Measure width from side to side at the widest point. Check for tapering: measure width at the top and bottom separately if they differ. Record thickness, especially if the cushion is down-filled or compressible. 3. Corner and L-Shaped Cushions These require extra attention due to their geometry. Lay the cushion flat and identify the angle (usually 90 degrees). Measure both arms of the L-shape independently: record length and depth for each section. Note the internal corner radius if rounded. Take diagonal measurements from outer corners to verify symmetry. 4. Round or Oval Cushions For round cushions, measure the diameter across the widest point. For ovals, measure both the longest and shortest diameters. Always include thickness, as deep cushions need more fabric for side panels. Tip: For tufted or buttoned cushions, measure between buttons to capture indentations that affect fabric drape. Do’s and Don’ts When Measuring for Covers Do’s Don’ts Measure at multiple points and average if needed Assume all cushions are the same size Write down measurements immediately Estimate without using a tape measure Account for seam allowances (add ½” per side) Add excessive extra inches “just in case” Measure compressed cushions as they sit in use Measure while the cushion is still on the sofa frame Use rigid rulers for straight edges, tape for curves Stretch the tape measure too tightly Real-World Example: Fixing a Fit Issue Sarah from Portland ordered new linen covers for her sectional’s seat cushions. She re-measured each cushion and discovered that years of use had flattened the foam by nearly ¾ inch in depth—but because she initially measured only one cushion, she missed variations across the set. After remeasuring all six cushions individually and adjusting for current dimensions, she reordered with updated specs. The second batch fit perfectly, lying smoothly without tension. Her experience underscores two critical lessons: always measure every cushion, and account for wear-related compression.

The cushions are flat, lumpy, or just plain worn out-but the frame still holds up fine. You’re not alone. Most people think replacing a whole sofa is the only answer. But here’s the truth: couch cushions can and should be replaced on their own. It’s cheaper, faster, and way more sustainable than tossing the whole thing. Why Replace Just the Cushions? Your sofa’s frame is usually made of hardwood or metal. These last 15 to 20 years if treated right. The cushions? They’re the weak link. Foam breaks down after 3 to 7 years. Fabric fades, stains, or gets stretched out. Down fills clump. You don’t need a new sofa-you need new cushions. In Auckland, where humidity and heavy use wear out furniture fast, replacing cushions is a common fix. A local upholstery shop told me they do 12 cushion replacements for every full sofa rebuild. That’s because the frame stays solid. The cushions? They’re the first to go. What Parts of the Cushion Can You Replace? Not all cushions are the same. Here’s what you can swap out: Foam core: The main support. Most sagging comes from low-density foam turning to mush. High-resilience (HR) foam lasts longer and holds shape better. Down or fiberfill wrap: The soft layer around the foam. It adds comfort but doesn’t provide support. If it’s clumpy or thin, replace it. Cushion cover: The outer fabric. If it’s stained, torn, or faded, you can get it reupholstered or buy a new slipcover. Inserts: Some cushions have removable inner cores. These are the easiest to swap-just unzip and pull out. How to Measure Your Cushions for Replacement You can’t just buy any cushion. It has to fit your sofa perfectly. Here’s how to get the right size: Remove the cushion from the sofa. Measure the length, width, and thickness with a tape measure. Write it down. Check the shape. Is it square, rectangular, or rounded? Take a photo. Look at the attachment. Are there ties? Zippers? Buttons? Note how it’s secured. Measure the depth of the sofa seat where the cushion sits. Some cushions are designed to sit flush, others to sink in slightly. Pro tip: Don’t guess. Even a half-inch difference can make the cushion look crooked or leave gaps. If you’re unsure, take the old cushion to a local upholstery shop. They’ll match it for you. Choosing the Right Foam Density Foam density is measured in pounds per cubic foot (PCF). It’s not about softness-it’s about durability. Low density (1.5-1.8 PCF): Cheap, soft, flattens fast. Found in budget sofas. Avoid. Medium density (1.8-2.5 PCF): Standard for most mid-range sofas. Lasts 5-7 years. High density (2.5-3.0+ PCF): Firm, supportive, lasts 10+ years. Best for daily use. If you sit on your sofa for hours, go with high-density foam. If it’s for light use or a guest room, medium works. For the best combo of comfort and longevity, choose HR foam with a 2.8 PCF rating. It’s the sweet spot. Down vs. Fiberfill: What’s Better? Many cushions have a layer of down or fiberfill wrapped around the foam. This makes the seat feel plush, not hard. Down: Feels luxurious, molds to your body, but needs fluffing. Can clump or leak if the fabric tears. Requires a higher thread count cover. Fiberfill (polyester): Easier to maintain, doesn’t clump, hypoallergenic. Doesn’t last as long as down but is cheaper and more consistent. If you want luxury and don’t mind maintenance, go with down. If you want easy care and don’t mind a slightly less plush feel, fiberfill is smarter. Most people choose fiberfill today-it’s more practical. Can You Buy Replacement Cushions Online?

These rounded corners allow the cushion to fit neatly inside the woven shape of the chair. When measuring this style cushion: Measure the full width of the cushion from left to right. Determine If the Furniture Uses Multiple Cushions Many wicker seating pieces use separate cushions rather than one large cushion. Measure finished top size: Measure the visible top surface, not the fully stretched size. Photograph the underside: The tuft buttons are often visible from the bottom, and this photo helps a maker reproduce the pattern. Pro tip: For any cushion that sits inside a frame, measure the frame's interior opening. A cushion measured from the outside of the frame will almost always be too big. Handling Odd Shapes and Custom Configurations Some outdoor seating is simply not a rectangle. L-shaped sectionals, curved banquettes, and chaise lounges with built-in wedge sections require a different strategy. Trace it: Place the cushion on a large sheet of butcher paper or cardboard. Trace the exact perimeter with a marker. This gives you a precise template that no list of numbers can match. Grid it: Place the traced paper on a grid (1-inch or 2-inch squares). Count the squares and note the coordinates of the corners. This is a technique patterns makers use, and it translates perfectly to cushion making. Photograph with scale: Place a ruler or a standard 8.5 x 11 inch piece of paper next to the cushion when you photograph it. This gives the manufacturer a visual reference for proportion. When you order a custom shape, always mention whether your measurements represent the interior cover size or the finished exterior size. Many vendors need you to specify this, and getting it wrong is the most common reason for a "custom" cushion that doesn't fit. Tracing odd shapes onto paper yields a template far more accurate than any list of measurements. Source: cascadiaoutdoorcushions.com Measure the Frame, Not Just the Cushion This is where experience separates good measurers from great ones. A new cushion should fit the frame, not necessarily match the old cushion's exact dimensions. Old cushions lose their structure. An old cushion with flattened foam might measure 21 inches deep, but the frame opening is 20 inches. If you replace with a new 21-inch cushion, it will bulge and strain against the frame. Always measure the interior of the frame where the cushion will reside. Measure the opening's width and depth. Then measure your existing cushion. If the cushion has stretched or sagged, you'll likely want to order closer to the frame dimensions, or possibly a half-inch smaller to allow for the new cushion's plumpness. Extra Measurements That Matter The basic width, depth, and thickness are just the starting point. Savvy buyers also check: Diagonal length: For a square cushion, measure across the diagonal. If this measurement is off, your "square" cushion is actually a parallelogram, and it won't sit flush in a square frame. Tie and strap placement: High winds and active kids mean many outdoor cushions use ties to stay in place. Measure the distance of the ties from the edges of the cushion. If replacement ties are at a different location than your frame's anchor points, the new cushion won't secure properly. Zipper placement: The zipper can sit on the bottom, the back edge, or the side. For a replacement cover, note the zipper's exact location and length. Lay the pad down on a flat surface. Measure the width of the pad from one side to another at the FRONT edge. Measure the width of the pad from one side to another at the REAR edge. The Golden Rule: Measure the Cover, Not the Foam Always measure the fabric shell from seam to seam because old foam compresses and loses its original shape, leading to inaccurate dimensions. When learning how to measure couch cushions for replacement, the most frequent mistake DIYers make is pulling the measuring tape across the existing foam core. This is a fundamental error because polyurethane foam is subject to the Seam-to-Seam Compression Factor. Over years of use, the cellular structure of the foam breaks down, causing it to lose its "memory" and physical volume. If you measure the foam itself, you are essentially measuring a failed component that has shrunk, which will result in a replacement that fits loosely and looks amateur. The fabric cover, however, acts as the "source of truth." Unlike foam, the textile structure of a high-quality upholstery cover typically retains its original dimensions. By measuring the shell, you are identifying the maximum volume the cover can hold. This ensures that the new foam will properly fill the fabric from corner to corner, eliminating the unsightly "puddling" or sagging often seen in poorly executed replacements. Remove foam from cover: Unzip the casing and carefully extract the old insert to ensure the fabric can lie flat. Turn cover inside out: This allows you to see the actual stitch lines and seam allowances clearly. Pull fabric taut but not stretched: You want to remove wrinkles and slack without distorting the natural shape of the textile. Locate the exact seam line: Your measurement must start and end exactly where the two pieces of fabric are joined. By focusing on the internal dimensions of the casing rather than the external dimensions of the degraded foam, you guarantee a precision fit that mimics original manufacturer standards. Professionals always rely on the "skin" of the cushion to dictate the "skeleton" inside. The fabric cover represents the maximum capacity of your cushion; the foam inside does not. Once you have the cover prepared, you must identify the three core dimensions. Step-by-Step Dimensions: Width, Depth, and Thickness Measure the width from left to right, the depth from front to back, and the thickness between the top and bottom welt cords. To achieve a professional result when determining how to measure couch cushions for replacement, you must treat the cushion as a three-dimensional geometric box. Precision is paramount, as even a half-inch discrepancy can lead to cushions that either overlap awkwardly or leave "black holes" between the seats where debris and remote controls disappear. You should always use a firm metal measuring tape rather than a flexible tailor’s tape to avoid inaccuracies caused by tape sag. The width is the measurement taken across the front face of the cushion from the left seam to the right seam. It is critical to measure both the front and the back width, as some cushions taper slightly toward the rear. The depth is the distance from the front nose of the cushion to the back zipper seam. Finally, the thickness or "loft" is measured between the piping (also known as welt cords). If your cushion does not have piping, measure between the top and bottom seams while holding the fabric vertical and taut. This is the space that the foam core must fill to keep the top and bottom fabric surfaces tight. If your cover has a 5-inch side wall, your base foam should reflect that dimension before adding any necessary wrap or batting. Measuring at the widest and deepest points accounts for the natural curve of the cushion and ensures that the replacement core will provide edge-to-edge support. Measuring Specialty Shapes: T-Cushions and L-Cushions For T-shaped or L-shaped cushions, divide the cover into a main rectangular body and separate extension segments to calculate the total foam footprint. Specialty shapes often intimidate DIYers, but the secret to success is deconstruction. A T-cushion or an L-cushion is simply a collection of rectangles joined together. How to Measure Replacement Cushions If you are replacing old or worn outdoor cushions and the original cushions are still intact enough to measure, measuring the old cushion directly is often the most reliable method. Measuring an Existing Cushion Place the old cushion on a flat surface. Measure the width across the top surface at the widest point. Measure the depth from front to back at the deepest point. Measure the thickness from the top surface to the bottom at the thickest point. If the old cushion has compressed significantly with age, its current thickness may be less than the original. Consider ordering a slightly thicker cushion if you want to restore the original comfort level. When the Old Cushion Is No Longer Usable If the old cushion is too worn to measure accurately, measure the furniture frame directly using the steps above for the relevant furniture type. If you have a label or tag from the original cushion that shows the size, use that as a starting reference and confirm against the frame measurement. Common Measuring Mistakes to Avoid These are the most frequent errors people make when measuring for outdoor cushions. Mistake 1: Measuring the Outside of the Frame The most common mistake is measuring the total outer width or depth of the furniture, rather than the inner seating area. The cushion needs to fit inside the frame, not match the frame's total outer dimensions. Always measure the inside of the frame — the actual area where the cushion will sit. Mistake 2: Only Measuring Width, Not Depth Many people measure the width of the seat but forget to measure the depth. A cushion that is the right width but too short or too deep front-to-back will either fall off the seat or bunch up against the back frame. Always measure both dimensions. Mistake 3: Not Accounting for Armrest Cutouts On some bench and loveseat designs, armrests are positioned within the seating area. A standard rectangular cushion will not fit correctly around these armrests. If your furniture has armrests that interrupt the seating surface, you need a cushion with cutouts or notches. Note the position and size of the armrest posts when ordering or contacting us. Mistake 4: Assuming Standard Sizes Fit Even furniture from well-known brands does not always use standard cushion sizes. Manufacturing tolerances, older models, and international brands can all result in dimensions that fall outside standard cushion sizes. Measure your furniture directly rather than assuming a standard size will fit. Mistake 5: Rounding Up Too Much It is generally better to use your exact measurement or round down slightly rather than rounding up. A cushion that is slightly too large will overhang the frame and look and feel off. If your measurement falls between whole inches, round down to the nearest half inch for a snug fit. Mistake 6: Forgetting to Measure Thickness Thickness affects how the cushion looks and feels, and also affects how it fits within the chair frame. Some chairs have armrests at a fixed height — a cushion that is too thick may sit above the armrest level, which feels awkward. Consider the relationship between cushion thickness and armrest height when choosing thickness for chairs with fixed armrests. 9. What to Do If Your Size Is Non-Standard If your measurements do not match an available ready-to-ship size, begin with a custom configuration using the width, depth and thickness you recorded. For straight rectangular seating, enter the measurements shown on the relevant custom product page and review the current options before adding to cart. For angled corners, curves, posts, cutouts or another unusual feature, do not assume a standard rectangle will fit. Keep a photo and a simple sketch with your measurements, then confirm the appropriate configuration before ordering. Have your measurements ready?
